We study whether frontier large language models (LLMs) exhibit prospect-theoretic framing patterns in risky choice and how their risk posture compares with – and shapes – that of humans in business-relevant contexts. In two preregistered between-subjects discrete-choice experiments, a panel of 17 LLMs and 1029 human participants evaluated four numerically equivalent gain–loss framing scenarios, chose between a certain option and a probabilistic one, and provided a brief justification. Most frontier reasoning and chat models favored certainty in 87%–100% of trials across frames and contexts, substantially attenuating the classic gain–loss reversal, while lighter-weight models exhibited greater human-like framing sensitivity and, in some cases, extreme risk-seeking. Human participants reproduced the classic framing effect with modest variation across scenarios. When shown a “committee of advisors” recommendation aggregated from the first experiment, however, human choices shifted sharply toward certainty in both frames – by 8.3 to 15.5 percentage points in the gain frame and 25.1 to 37.3 in the loss frame, controlling for risk preferences and other factors. Topic modeling of justifications shows that unadvised humans drew on moral and responsibility-based reasoning essentially absent from LLM output; under AI advice, that vocabulary receded and certainty- and probability-based language expanded – humans began to sound like the LLMs. Deploying an LLM as a decision aid is thus not a neutral upgrade: it imports a model-specific distribution of risk recommendations and delegates not only the choice but the framing of the decision itself, with direct implications for AI governance.

documents.abstract: Abstract The rate at which collaborative robots (cobots) are evolving from isolated, pre-programmed manipulators into collaborative partners that operate productively alongside humans, other robots, and machines is accelerating rapidly. Advances in computer vision is enabling cobots, even in dynamic and cluttered settings, to detect, recognise and assess both environment and actions. However, achieving higher detection accuracy and real-time localization in dynamic systems remains a challenge, as most existing approaches assume uncluttered backgrounds with limited scene complexity. Closing this gap is critical for both research and industrial deployment. This paper reviews the development of visual perception in cobots, surveys emerging computer vision algorithms, and examines a holistic perception pipeline in which raw vision signals, vision language models (VLMs), and augmented/virtual reality interfaces jointly power a unified sense-think-act loop. The review finds that cobots in high-mix, reconfigurable factories face serious challenges: occlusions in fields of view, fluctuating illumination, ambiguous backgrounds, few- or zero-shot object scenarios, high-speed motion, and computational problems in fusing heterogeneous data streams in real time. Cobots also need to manipulate damaged items, requiring vision algorithms that infer geometry from sparse cues and support adaptive grasping. Finally, the review identifies three complementary research directions to unlock plug-and-play cobots: (1) information aware sensor-fusion pipelines transmitting only credible voxels to reduce bandwidth while preserving sub-millimetre accuracy; (2) language conditioned planning and control networks mapping plain-language goals to smooth, jerk-bounded trajectories; and (3) pre-trained few-shot reward heads that score task progress without bespoke metrics, closing the reinforcement learning (RL) loop. Combined, these advances promise cobots that can be commissioned with relatively few demonstrations.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly proposed as a decision-support layer inside operational management systems, yet many such systems disclose neither the provenance of their recommendations nor a mechanism by which a manager can govern their consequences before they take effect. This chapter addresses that governance problem through SmartTransit OS, a prototype public-transit operating system built and examined here as a governance testbed rather than as a finished management product. The system unifies four role-scoped portals — Passenger, Driver, Administrator/Operations, and System Operations Center — around one authentication system and one shared operational state. Software events are communicated in real time, but vehicle telemetry is simulated. Server-enforced, field-level role-based access control governs what each role may see and change. Every automatically generated decision-support output, covering estimated arrival time, occupancy, and operational anomalies, carries an explicit provenance label identifying it as a rule-engine, hybrid, database, or simulation output, and authorized personnel may review recommendations, with decisions recorded in an audit log. The prototype does not enforce completion of review and does not execute recommendations automatically; any operational change requires a separate authorized human action. The chapter argues that the decision-support layer's current deterministic, rule-based design is a deliberate methodological choice: it isolates the governance mechanisms — authorization, shared state, provenance, human approval, and auditability — from the additional uncertainty a trained model would introduce, allowing their specified behavior to be examined separately before any such model is introduced. The demonstration dataset is small and seeded, and the prototype has not been integrated with real GPS/AVL hardware, GTFS-Realtime feeds, ticketing systems, or external transit operators; no field deployment or independent security audit has been conducted. Evaluation is architectural and qualitative, supplemented by author-reported synthetic boundary-case counts that do not measure operational performance. The chapter concludes that this governance pattern does not depend on the underlying decision-support method and would remain relevant if future versions of the system introduce trained models for prediction, anomaly detection, or dispatch.

Solving new large language model (LLM) and robotic based oncology clinical trial industry problems requires proper publication of protocols, standards, legislation, and funding applications prior to deployment. This paper provides solution sets derived from prior author works for upcoming Physical SI (super intelligence) oncology trials. The publications referenced here require whole implementation, as capabilities differ between state-of-the-art AI models and robots per problem type. Many AI manufacturers’ models have been tested between 2024-2025 in order to discover novel and useful clinical trial applications. These developments include the creation of a patient matching machine learning pipeline, the combination of generated clinical trial meta-analyses to provide new AI insights for indications and cancer drugs, emerging clinical trial simulations, and accelerating the speed and quality of the academic paper creation process. Ultimately, 2026 multi-prompt processes have been optimized to single master prompt systems featured in new trial protocols, drug applications, and funding requests - which feature autonomous AI sub-prompt generation and execution, professional machine readable diagrams, and iterations of full academic paper source code files using a repository-based LLM. Resulting single master prompt-based publications contained high contextual awareness, with a limited number of author corrections required for diagram positioning and paper formatting. Two comprehensive LLM and oncology clinical trial literature reviews conducted in 2025 and 2026 yielded a limited number applications, delayed implementations of new AI models - prompting the oncology trial solutions.

documents.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the conditions under which a European organization can adopt a permissively licensed language model, develop it further within a confidential environment, retain control over its model weights and training materials, and reduce dependence on NVIDIA hardware and other concentrated infrastructure suppliers. The analysis combines a targeted review of model releases and license terms, an assessment of European Union and national legal requirements, a threat-model-based security architecture, and a staged procurement and development roadmap. The study forms part of the broader intellectual and research context of Omegacene, an interdisciplinary project examining the implications of artificial intelligence, technological transformation, and the changing relationship between human and machine agency. Within this context, AI sovereignty is treated not merely as a question of model ownership or infrastructure procurement, but as a problem of institutional control, verifiable accountability, and the capacity to make consequential technological systems independently assessable and governable. The central finding is that model licensing, regulatory compliance, operational security, and supply-chain sovereignty are separate but interdependent dimensions. Apache License 2.0 generally permits confidential modification without an obligation to publish derivative artifacts. This permission does not establish the lawfulness of training data, guarantee freedom from third-party rights, or exempt a downstream organization from applicable AI, data protection, cybersecurity, or procurement law. The European Commission’s compute-based guidance on modifications of general-purpose AI models provides a useful planning indicator, but it does not constitute a statutory exemption or a security threshold. Technical transparency can improve auditability but cannot prove the absence of malicious behavior. Confidential execution, access controls, artifact signing, and model-extraction defenses reduce particular risks without providing absolute protection. Hardware independence is likewise multidimensional: replacing NVIDIA with another supplier does not eliminate dependence on non-European fabrication, memory, interconnects, firmware, or design tools. Advanced fabrication already exists within the EU, but the evidence reviewed does not establish a complete, independently controllable European accelerator supply chain. The paper proposes three complementary model-development tracks, a four-zone security architecture, measurable procurement requirements, corrected compute estimates, and a risk register. Its principal contribution is a framework for making sovereignty claims testable by translating broad aspirations into explicit technical, legal, operational, and supply-chain criteria. In the wider Omegacene.com context, this approach offers a practical basis for evaluating whether control over AI systems is substantive, demonstrable, and resilient, rather than merely asserted through licensing choices or national affiliation. Keywords: digital sovereignty; general-purpose AI; Apache License 2.0; AI Act; confidential model development; model weights; trade secrets; confidential computing; export controls; semiconductor supply chains; EuroHPC; public procurement.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Digital transformation has intensified the need for organizations to align workforce strategy, digital commerce systems, and intelligent marketing capabilities. This comprehensive review examines how strategic human resource management, digital commerce, and AI-driven marketing support sustainable business growth and organizational performance. The review synthesizes literature on digital workforce planning, reskilling, platform-based commerce, marketing automation, predictive analytics, customer personalization, employee engagement, organizational resilience, and ethical governance. The findings indicate that strategic human resource management provides the capability foundation by developing digital skills, adaptive leadership, cross-functional collaboration, and continuous learning. Digital commerce serves as the value-creation and delivery infrastructure through online platforms, fintech integration, omnichannel systems, and network-based business models. AI-driven marketing serves as the customer-intelligence mechanism by enabling segmentation, forecasting, automation, personalization, and real-time engagement. Their coordinated integration can strengthen innovation, productivity, customer experience, revenue generation, and resilience. However, sustainable outcomes depend on reliable data, employee trust, human oversight, privacy protection, algorithmic fairness, and accountable governance. The review proposes an integrated framework linking people, commerce, and marketing capabilities through innovation, efficiency, engagement, and customer value. Future research should empirically test this framework across industries, firm sizes, and national contexts using longitudinal and standardized performance measures. It identifies research priorities concerning human–AI collaboration, digital inclusion, and environmental performance measurement.

In the contemporary era, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into education, influencing how students learn, engage, and accomplish academic tasks. This study examined students’ perceptions of AI along two distinct dimensions: utilization and regulation to serve as an evidence-based basis for developing institutional guidelines. Specifically, it addressed four areas of utilization: AI literacy, academic writing support, personalized learning, and student engagement; and two areas of regulation: awareness of AI policies, rules and regulations, and academic integrity and ethical concerns. A descriptive research design was employed, using a survey questionnaire administered to 229 students from the Teacher Education Program at the Polytechnic College of the City of Meycauayan. Data were collected through online and printed forms and analyzed using descriptive statistics, specifically weighted mean, to determine general trends in students’ responses. On utilization, students generally perceived AI as a useful educational tool that enhances learning efficiency, supports academic writing tasks, and enables personalized, self-paced learning. They demonstrated moderate to high AI literacy, with strong awareness of potential misuse and privacy risks, though some reported difficulty learning new AI tools. Usage varied across platforms: Canva, ChatGPT, and Grammarly were the most familiar and widely used, while other tools had limited adoption. On regulation, students expressed strong support for institutional policies, rules, and accountability frameworks. They showed high awareness of ethical standards, data privacy, fairness, and responsible use. yet were less supportive of mandatory disclosure of AI assistance in academic work. Concerns about over-reliance, the absence of clear existing rules, and the urgent need for formal guidance were clearly evident. The study concludes that while AI offers significant educational benefits, comprehensive institutional guidelines on AI utilization and regulation are urgently needed to ensure responsible, ethical, and equitable use. Recommendations include integrating AI literacy training, establishing level-based usage policies, requiring transparency in AI assistance, and upholding academic integrity through clear ethical standards. These findings provide a data-driven foundation for balanced institutional policies that support innovation while maintaining academic integrity and fairness.

Teacher’s Guide to the AI-Driven Classroom Toolkit is a practical resource for building teachers’ capacity to use artificial intelligence responsibly and effectively in teaching and learning. Developed for educators, the toolkit introduces foundational concepts in artificial intelligence, digital literacy, prompt engineering, AI-supported lesson planning, assessment, differentiated instruction, student engagement, and reflective teaching practice. It also presents practical guidance for working in low-resource environments with limited access to devices and reliable internet connectivity. The toolkit discusses responsible and ethical AI use, including accuracy verification, data privacy, academic integrity, bias awareness, fairness, inclusion, transparency, and the continuing importance of teacher judgment and human oversight. It highlights AI as a support tool that can enhance teaching efficiency and learning experiences without replacing the professional, relational, and ethical responsibilities of educators. The resource is intended for teachers, teacher educators, education administrators, professional-development facilitators, researchers, and other stakeholders interested in practical AI integration in schools.

documents.abstract: This is a theoretical paper that evaluates the correlation between the nonverbal immediacy behaviors of the teachers and the intrinsic motivation of students undertaking General Foundation Programs (GFP) in tertiary education using the Immediacy Theory by Mehrabian as the main point of analysis. Nonverbal immediacy operationalized in terms of behaviors including eye contact, gestures, facial expressions, vocal variety, and physical proximity has been repeatedly linked with positive affective learning experiences in a variety of educational settings. This paper will use the Immediacy Theory which suggests that communicative behaviors that lead to minimization of psychological distance create relational closeness and positive affect to explain how behaviors can be used to develop intrinsic motivation in GFP students. The GFP context is a special pedagogical context where students who have left secondary and started their higher education often come across linguistic, academic and psychological demands, making teacher immediacy more consequential. The presented paper is a narrative literature review of both empirical and theoretical articles published in 2000-2024 that have been identified by applying a set of preset inclusion and exclusion criteria via a systematic search of ERIC, Google Scholar, and JSTOR databases. The review incorporates the discoveries in the spheres of communication, educational psychology and second-language acquisition to develop a conceptual framework of how teacher nonverbal immediacy is related to increased intrinsic motivation, and the quality of teacher-student relationships is suggested as a critical mediating variable. The paper ends with conclusions about practical implications to GFP instructors, institutional stakeholders, and the future empirical research directions.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into in these aspects of educational environments has initiated more of a paradigm shift in pedagogical structural methodologies, assessment strategies, and the use of fundamental role of educators. This comprehensive review always seems to be examined the current state of teaching competency in the age of AI, focusing here on three pivotal dimensions: teachers' attitudes towards AI, their adaptability of such aspects in utilizing intelligent tools, and their professional commitment in an era of rapid technological disruption-based aspects. Drawing upon a more natured based synthesis of recent literature, we therefore explore how factors such as AI literacy, generative based AI competence, & as also AI-TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge) influence here in the successful integration of AI into classrooms everywhere. The review in this aspects highlights that while educators here are increasingly by recognizing the potential of AI to more enhance personalized learning as well as administrative efficiency, there remain in this way to stay neutral significant barriers related to AI anxiety as also, ethical concerns, & most of all a lack of targeted based on professional development. Adaptability is conceptualized not merely as herein technical proficiency, but as a continuous pedagogical evolution requiring robust organizational support-based aspects. Furthermore, professional aspects of commitment in this nature always is analyzed through the lens of shifting teacher identities & the ethical imperative to foster critical thinking and human-centric values based through in AI-augmented learning environments. A prominent table-based data related structure is provided to synthesize the thematic findings, mapping core competencies and against professional development needs. The paper in this manner concludes with actionable recommendations for policymakers, teacher training programs, & future research directions to ensure that educators are adequately equipped here to navigate the complexities of AI in education.

documents.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reorganizing the ecology in which cognition, social understanding, agency, authorship, and emotional regulation develop. This critical integrative review treats GenAI as a developmentally consequential interactive artifact: responsive, adaptive, linguistically fluent, multimodal, and increasingly embedded in learning, play, and communication. Drawing on sociocultural, constructivist, ecological, extended-cognition, AI-literacy, and hybrid-learning perspectives, we introduce the Hybrid Mind Framework. It defines human-AI coupling as recurrent, contingent coordination and distinguishes immediate AI-supported performance from durable changes in unaided competence, competence during coupling, trust, support-seeking, or authorship. Four domains are considered: cognitive hybridization, social-epistemic calibration, affective scaffolding and support-seeking, and agency/authorship. The review integrates emerging GenAI evidence with research on earlier responsive technologies and differentiates early childhood, middle childhood, early adolescence, and later adolescence. Existing evidence indicates possible short-term affordances and risks, but long-term developmental effects remain largely untested. Rather than treating GenAI as either a pedagogical miracle or a developmental threat, we propose that AI be designed and governed as part of children's developmental ecology. Testable propositions and age-calibrated implications distinguish observed findings from theory-derived and precautionary claims.

In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has seen a significant growth in its integration with the field of Education. This has started many concerns about the effect it has on the process of learning, academic integrity and skill development. This paper examines the effects of AI use within the context of higher education institutions, as it investigates Moroccan postgraduate students’ perceptions on their academic achievements. The targeted sample consisted of 15 postgraduate students enrolled in the English departments of two public universities. This research follows a qualitative approach, as it aims to capture the students’ experience of AI use in their academic life. The findings highlight potential risks of heavy reliance on AI, which include a diminished confidence in the students’ performance, reduced engagement in independent learning and more. However, AI also presents many opportunities for enhancing the process of learning and education when used as a complementary tool instead of replacing the whole cognitive process. This study puts an emphasis on the need for a balanced AI integration while focusing on the development of the students’ cognitive skills in the process. This study contributes to the persisting debate regarding the implementation of AI tools in education and examines how they can be used ethically without diminishing students’ efforts or undermining their original contributions.

documents.abstract: The Job Is No Longer the Whole StoryDiscussions about artificial intelligence and the future of work often begin with a familiar question: Which jobs will machines replace?The question is understandable because organizations are structured around jobs.Recruitment, compensation, performance appraisal, workforce planning, and organizational hierarchies are generally built around positions occupied by people.Yet a job is not the work itself.A job is a formal organizational container within which many different activities are performed.A customer-support agent may receive a customer request, interpret the problem, search for information, formulate a response, communicate with the customer, document the interaction, escalate unusual cases, and accept responsibility for the outcome.A warehouse employee may locate inventory, move material, scan products, replenish locations, verify orders, and resolve exceptions.A management consultant may collect information, analyze data, develop alternatives, prepare presentations, communicate with clients, and exercise professional judgment.These activities differ substantially in their information requirements, physical requirements, variability, and need for human judgment.This distinction becomes important as artificial intelligence, autonomous AI agents, robotics, and other intelligent systems become capable of performing selected components of organizational work.Technology does not necessarily encounter a job as a single indivisible object.It encounters activities and tasks.

Foundation Program students often struggle to generate research ideas and organise their thoughts when writing research-based essays, which can undermine their confidence and academic performance. Traditional assessment methods provide limited insight into students' independent development of ideas. However, recent advances in educational technology, particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI), offer new opportunities to support learning. This study aims to investigate the pedagogical impact of AI-assisted idea generation on General Foundation Program (GFP) students' self-efficacy and idea-generating skills in research-based essay writing. The study adopts a quantitative research design using a single-group pre-test and post-test approach. The sample consists of 25 randomly selected GFP students. The intervention is conducted over a period of 4-6 weeks. Students use ChatGPT as their primary AI tool for brainstorming, outlining, and refining ideas. Students' self-efficacy is measured based on a structured questionnaire, while idea development skills are assessed through a writing rubric. Data is analysed using paired-sample comparison. The results indicate improvement in both self-efficacy and idea development. The study highlights the importance of integrating AI tools into writing instruction to enhance student confidence and performance.

Artificial intelligence is expanding rapidly across energy systems, offering tools for renewable integration, forecasting, grid reliability, and demand management while also increasing electricity and infrastructure demand. Yet evidence of its energy-system benefits remains fragmented across national contexts and is often synthesised without accounting for differences in evidence quality or governance. This study addresses that gap through a systematic review of 146 peer-reviewed studies and authoritative reports published from 2010 to 2026, supplemented by earlier foundational methodological sources dating back to 1994. It compares the United States, India, South Korea, and Sweden, selected to represent contrasting market-led, emerging-economy, state-directed, and mature low-carbon contexts. The analysis combines an evidence-tiered comparison across 14 energy-system indicators, a city-level deployment index covering ten urban centres, and a four-pillar governance framework. Reported studies indicate improvements in renewable-energy forecasting performance, while CNN-based and explainable machine-learning approaches have been applied to power-system fault detection; however, country-specific quantitative validation remains uneven. Northern Virginia/DC ranks first with an unrounded AECDI score of 83.00, followed closely by Stockholm at 82.95; both scores round to 83 for presentation, but they achieve these results through different pathways: infrastructure scale and grid deployment in Northern Virginia/DC, and low-carbon electricity integration and institutional maturity in Stockholm. Across the four cases, technical performance and investment alone do not ensure sustainable outcomes; grid carbon intensity, institutional capacity, cybersecurity, explainability, and equity shape how benefits are realised. The study contributes a transparent and replicable approach that links evidence quality, sub-national deployment patterns, and measurable governance priorities, providing practical guidance for more effective and equitable integration of artificial intelligence into energy systems.

ABSTRACT: There is one essential aspect of HRM practices that improves the performance of employees: their relationship with job characteristics. In HRM practices that include selection, induction, training, performance evaluation, and compensation, plus the development and maintenance of engagement, employees are seen, when combined with the significant job attributes, to develop great outcomes. The Job Characteristics Model is a valuable resource, as its principles would relate to skill variety, task identity, significance of the task, autonomy, and feedback. Therefore, within jobs that excite, challenge, motivate, and inspire employees, an organization can design or redesign jobs so they support employee engagement and better performance. When HRM practice is combined with well-designed job characteristics, it positively motivates employees in their work since well-designed job characteristics also contribute to employee motivation. Literature observed that HRM practices are said to have a positive impact on job satisfaction and organizational commitment. This proves the existence of relationships that mediate to ensure better productivity and performance of employees. Moreover, organizations that combine strategic HRM practices and job design in support are much more likely than others to realize improved organizational development and enhancement of innovation strategies. Hence, HRM alignment with job design is an inevitable factor that will surely enhance the performance of both individuals and organizations. KEYWORDS: HRM Practices, Job Characteristics, Employee Performance, Motivation, Job Satisfaction, Organizational Commitment.

Abstract Background Artificial Intelligence (AI) promises to improve patient outcomes, increase efficiency, and reduce healthcare costs. While AI has demonstrated success in imaging fields like radiology, its application is expanding into other data-rich medical domains, including neonatology. Nonetheless, a disparity persists between technical advancements of AI and its practical use in clinical care. A significant obstacle for integrating these systems into bedside decision-making is physicians’ difficulty in determining when AI can reasonably be trusted. Methods We explored the perspectives of neonatologists at a Dutch academic hospital on trust in AI via in-depth, semi-structured interviews ( n = 17). Thematic analysis was used to identify key themes. Results Three overarching themes emerged: (1) Trusting AI in practice, (2) Maintaining control over trusted AI systems, and (3) Limits of trust. Overall, AI in neonatal clinical settings was welcomed. The concept of trust was delineated as being distinct from that of confidence and reliance. For trusting AI, it was deemed important that AI’s role would be supplemental to the role of the physician. Also, AI validation and adequate oversight were considered essential for physicians’ trust. Preserving human expertise while working with AI in clinical settings was deemed important. Concerns about overreliance and incompatibility of clinical intuition with AI in practice were frequently mentioned as reasons to lose trust in AI. Conclusion This study offers practical insights into how trust in medical AI is conceptualized by neonatologists and highlights key considerations for its acceptance. Clarifying what is expected of physicians in terms of reliance on AI at the bedside and formulating concrete guidance for trust in AI is recommended. Trial registration Not applicable. The research protocol was reviewed by the research quality control committee of the University Medical Center Utrecht and was deemed exempt from the Medical Research Involving Humans Act (research proposal no. 23U0364).

documents.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in professional university work, yet its significance cannot be inferred from individual prompts, outputs or nominal categories of use. This study examines how differently organised professional practices shape what practitioners do with GenAI and what changes, persists, or is reopened as GenAI-mediated work becomes part of continuing professional projects. Drawing on practitioner-led collaborative action research and the theory of practice architectures, we analyse a longitudinal corpus of documented GenAI-mediated interaction embedded in continuing professional projects across assessment and calibration, course development, validation and credit transfer, practicum supervision, academic supervision, and scholarly work. The findings show that professional knowing was practice-specific: what practitioners needed to distinguish and judge differed with professional project and practice architectures. Cross-practice comparison identified recurring but overlapping configurations linking professional grounds, material conditions and situated responsibility, while analytical work could be distributed to GenAI without professional mandate becoming symmetrical. Longitudinally, earlier GenAI-mediated formulations and documents could persist, be reopened, recontextualised or become consequential for later practising. Locally coherent generative work could also cease to serve a wider professional project without becoming factually false. The study therefore complicates accounts of human oversight centred on final output verification. Professional judgement was enacted throughout collaboration through negotiation, restriction, attribution, reopening, and project-level monitoring. The findings further suggest that disclosure categories or preserved chat histories do not by themselves make GenAI participation inspectable, raising implications for scholarly disclosure, student assessment, and the design of accountable AI-mediated knowledge work.

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence increasingly automates cognitive work, organizations face a new challenge: deciding where human judgment continues to create value. This paper examines how AI changes the relationship between human thought, organizational processes, and decision making. It explores why preserving human involvement is not always the same as preserving valuable judgment, and how organizations can deliberately determine when to rely on automation, human oversight, or a combination of both. The central argument is that when human thought is no longer required to perform the work, human judgment must be intentionally designed into the process.

documents.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence is moving digital retail from recommendation toward autonomous consumer representation. This research develops agentic retail representation capability as the perceived capacity to acquire retail intelligence, adapt choice strategies, preserve consumer goals, and execute bounded actions. The study includes a qualitative pretest, two scale validation samples, three experiments, and an independent category validation study, comprising 4680 quantitative participants and 210 qualitative respondents. Studies 1A and 1B assess four reflective dimensions combined as a formative composite. Study 2 finds higher delegation intention under a bundled capability intervention and statistical indirect associations through perceived diagnosticity and algorithm trust. Study 3 identifies expertise dependent responses across assortments jointly varying in size, priority information coverage, and displayed prices, preventing attribution to complexity alone. Study 4 finds stronger capability related trust under a bundled transparency intervention and higher authorization rates within an experimental shopping task. Study 5 examines measurement transportability and correspondence with independently coded agent activity. These findings concern perceived capability, measured reliance, and task authorization rather than verified commercial purchases. The contribution distinguishes functional capacity from reliance judgments and permission decisions while specifying the limits of measured mediation and bundled interventions. Retail applications require further validation with real payments, delivery, returns, and repeated consumer use.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly moving beyond analytical retail functions into product development, raising new questions about how consumers respond depending on where AI is positioned within the process. Across three studies with U.S. consumers in fashion-related contexts, this research examines how the task AI performs and how its role is framed shape consumer responses to products developed with AI involvement. Study 1 maps consumers’ perceptions of fashion-related tasks along a logic–intuition continuum and identifies trend forecasting as a logic-oriented task and design as an intuition-oriented task. Study 2 compares AI involvement in these two contrasting product-development tasks and finds lower purchase intention when AI is involved in design rather than trend forecasting, with heightened human identity threat accounting for part of this difference. Study 3 focuses on the intuition-oriented design context and shows that framing AI as complementing rather than replacing human designers is associated with lower identity threat and higher purchase intention. Together, the findings suggest that consumer responses depend not only on whether AI participates in product development, but also on where AI is positioned within the process and how its contribution relative to human creativity is framed. This research advances understanding of task-dependent responses to AI by identifying human identity threat as a mediator linking AI involvement to purchase intention and by showing how role framing can shape purchase intention when AI participates in creative work.

documents.abstract: Measuring AI by how much faster developers work is like judging electricity by how much faster it spun a steam-era factory. A fuller measure asks what new work becomes possible. We surveyed 331 software developers at Microsoft about what AI lets them do that they could not do before and analyzed their answers using reflexive thematic analysis with a human-in-the-loop, multi-model AI council. Developers described doing familiar work faster (Faster, 45%), undertaking work previously beyond their reach (Further, 36.9%), and taking on new kinds of work centered on building for and directing AI agents (Afresh, 12.4%). Across these accounts, learning and scaffolding ran in both directions: developers learned new skills with AI while externalizing their tacit knowledge as the context and standards that guide AI's work. Drawing on Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, we frame developers and AI as joint learners whose zones meet at the skill-judgment nexus: AI can supply skill faster than it can reliably judge its own work, and developers must continuously bridge that gap. Whether they do sets them on one of two paths. On one, developers' judgment grows alongside AI's skill, and they codify what they learn so the loop keeps turning. On the other, they become hollow orchestrators, approving work they can no longer judge and losing the identity and meaning they once drew from it. Based on our findings, we offer a two-way scaffolding playbook to help developers, teams, and tool builders take the first path.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping educational practices, requiring teachers to develop new competencies while navigating complex ethical considerations. This qualitative study explores the perceptions, practices, and orientations of 28 Lebanese schoolteachers regarding the integration of AI in school settings. Findings indicate that while a majority of participants reported familiarity with AI, only a limited proportion integrated AI into their instructional practices. Reported barriers included insufficient training, lack of institutional support, and concerns related to data privacy and ethical use. The analysis led to the identification of three qualitative orientations toward AI integration—reluctant users, early adopters, and critical skeptics—reflecting differentiated levels of readiness and engagement. The findings highlight the need for context-sensitive, pedagogically grounded, and ethically informed professional development to support sustainable AI integration in education.

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes higher education, learning support centers are uniquely positioned to intentionally assess whether if and how to best integrate AI tools into academic services. This session presents a 6-week project framework that was designed to: • Review the literature on critical AI literacy and training • Benchmark current best practices in AI policy, use, and integration alongside human-centered academic services • Examine student AI knowledge and use (needs assessment) • Identify and evaluate relevant AI tools or platforms The framework was developed within the Academic Success Center (ASC) at Nevada State University where Center peer educators (student employees) served as project leads and evaluators. This model offers a practical, research-informed pathway for institutions seeking to lead responsibly in AI-integrated learning support or other student services. Session activities include a walkthrough and discussion of the model structure, tools, challenges, and recommendations. Attendees will leave with: (1) a sample 6-week project roadmap, (2) a student-centered model for AI evaluation and pilot design, (3) learning frameworks grounded in critical AI literacy, (4) adaptable resources for assessment and decision-making, and (5) strategies for positioning students as co-creators in institutional/unit change

documents.abstract: Introduction With the deep integration of digitalization and generative artificial intelligence, artificial intelligence has transformed from a mere technical tool into a core collaborative partner within modern workplaces and human‑resource management. As an interdependent human‑AI working mode characterized by complementary task division, joint task accomplishment, complementary decision‑making, and continuous iterative interaction between employees and AI agents, AI‑employee collaboration is conceptually distinct from simple AI adoption, instrumental AI use, and AI‑assisted technical systems. Drawing on social cognitive theory, the present study aims to investigate how AI‑employee collaboration predicts employee innovation behavior, alongside the mediating role of self‑efficacy and the moderated‑mediation boundary condition of servant leadership. Methods Three‑wave time‑lagged questionnaire data were collected from 259 employees working in internet‑service, finance, and catering industries across Beijing and Jinan. Hierarchical regression and bootstrap approaches were adopted to test the proposed moderated‑mediation model. Results The results show that AI‑employee collaboration exerts a significant positive predictive effect on employee innovation behavior. Self‑efficacy partially mediates the relationship between AI‑employee collaboration and employee innovation behavior. Moreover, servant leadership positively moderates the link between AI‑employee collaboration and self‑efficacy and further strengthens the indirect predictive effect of AI‑employee collaboration on employee innovation behavior through self‑efficacy. Discussion This research enriches existing literature by providing incremental empirical evidence for the internal cognitive mechanism and contextual boundary of AI‑driven employee innovation. Theoretically, it unpacks the cognitive “black box” connecting AI‑employee collaboration and employee innovation and identifies servant leadership as a key situational contingency factor. Practically, these findings deliver concrete, actionable managerial insights for digitally transforming organizations to leverage AI tools and unlock employees’ innovative potential.

The study “A Study on the Influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Literacy on Career Readiness Among Young Adults in Chennai” aims to establish a connection between the level of awareness about AI and career readiness. The influence of artificial intelligence is increasing in all fields of activity, especially in the educational and professional spheres. Therefore, understanding the characteristics of this technology is becoming a vital skill for achieving employability in the future. The study uses a descriptive research design, with a primary data collection method. The data was gathered by distributing questionnaires among one hundred respondents who were selected using a convenience sampling technique. The data analysis involved the percentage analysis of the results, the weighted average of the responses, multiple linear regression, and Pearson’s correlation. The analysis focused on investigating the level of AI literacy, the factors that contribute to it, and the relationship between AI literacy and career readiness. The results of the study showed that the mean score for AI literacy is 3.61, while that of career readiness is 3.33. According to multiple regression analysis, such variables as peer, social, and professional interaction, and personal curiosity and self-learning were statistically significant predictors of AI literacy, with a score of approximately 66%. The results also showed that AI literacy and career readiness were positively correlated (r = 0.819, p < 0.001). The study established the significance of improving the level of knowledge and skills about artificial intelligence among young adults, which will increase their chances of being employed. This information can be useful for academic organizations and young people who intend to gain knowledge about AI to enhance their employability.

Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Augmented Reality (AR) systems has evolved AR from a passive visualization tool into an intelligent medium for dynamic task execution. For this new role, Intelligent Augmented Reality (IAR) systems must adapt user interfaces (UIs) in real-time to users’ cognitive and physical states, task requirements, and environmental constraints, which raises foundational questions: what design decisions contribute to useful adaptive interaction? To address this question, this paper presents a systematic review of IAR systems through the lens of interaction design at the intersection of AR technologies , AI integration , and User Experience (UX) considerations . After screening 798 peer-reviewed works, 241 full-text records were assessed for eligibility. We reviewed 24 IAR published works based on their interaction features, including proactivity versus reactivity and communication styles and modalities, as well as their types of adaptation and control dynamics. Analyzing these features led to the development of a taxonomy for Levels of Automation and a top-down design framework for adaptive UIs in IAR Systems. Our findings highlight the effectiveness of assistive interaction and semi-autonomous IAR systems that achieve a balanced integration of adaptive assistance with prioritizing user agency while also revealing a noticeable gap in implicit understanding within current IAR implementations.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly changing the way healthcare is delivered by supporting a more personalized and patient-centered approach to medicine. Personalized medicine combines information such as genetics, genomics, medical history, lifestyle, laboratory results, medical images, and continuous health data to help healthcare professionals make better decisions for individual patients. Its applications include disease risk prediction, AI-assisted medical imaging, genomic data interpretation, biomarker identification, personalized drug selection, pharmacogenomics, adaptive drug dosing, treatment response prediction, and remote patient monitoring through wearable and mobile health technologies. However, successful implementation requires careful data collection, preprocessing, feature selection, model development, validation, and continuous monitoring. Despite its benefits, AI-driven personalized medicine faces important challenges, including data privacy and security, poor data quality, limited diversity in datasets, algorithmic bias, lack of transparency, high implementation costs, and regulatory and ethical concerns. Future developments such as digital twins, generative AI, precision oncology, multi-omics integration, federated learning, and real-time adaptive treatment systems may further strengthen personalized healthcare. Overall, AI should complement rather than replace healthcare professionals, providing evidence-based support while keeping patient safety, fairness, privacy, and clinical judgment at the center of care.

documents.abstract: Virtual immersive learning platforms (VILPs), integrating immersive technologies, gamified design, and learning tools, enable meaningful engagement in learning while also creating possibilities for compulsive engagement. Drawing on a sociotechnical affordance perspective, this study examines how configurations of affordances are associated with meaningful and compulsive engagement and how these pathways vary across demographic conditions. Using a mixed-methods design, we first uncover the core affordances of VILPs and organize them within a sociotechnical perspective. We then employ a two-stage fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to examine affordance configurations associated with different engagement outcomes and the role of demographic conditions. The findings show that meaningful and compulsive engagement are associated with distinct combinations of affordances and these configurational patterns vary across demographic conditions. These findings advance understanding of VILP engagement by revealing the configurational pathways associated with meaningful and compulsive engagement and offering practical insights into designing more inclusive and responsible learning platforms.

AI agents are increasingly deployed as persistent digital actors that can reason, access enterprise knowledge, invoke tools, and execute business actions. Unlike conventional applications, agents may adapt their behavior dynamically and operate with varying levels of autonomy, making lifecycle governance essential. This paper proposes an AI Agent Lifecycle Governance Framework covering ideation, risk classification, design, data and model selection, identity, tool approval, development, testing, security review, Responsible AI evaluation, deployment, runtime monitoring, change management, recertification, suspension, and retirement. The framework integrates enterprise architecture, model risk management, cybersecurity, auditability, human oversight, and operational governance into a repeatable lifecycle. It defines governance gates, accountable roles, evidence requirements, runtime controls, and measurable KPIs/KRIs. The proposed approach enables enterprises to scale agentic AI responsibly while maintaining traceability, bounded authority, regulatory readiness, and long-term operational control.

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence reshapes virtually every field, universities face a growing imperative to ensure AI literacy is not reserved for computer science majors alone. This panel presents the collaborative design of an introductory AI course built for undergraduate general education — one that serves students across disciplines, regardless of technical background. Two co-designers will share the story of building the course from complementary angles. The first presenter will address the technical foundation of the curriculum: how core AI concepts such as machine learning, data, and algorithms were translated into accessible, hands-on learning experiences for non-specialist students. The second presenter will explore the philosophical framework woven throughout the course — examining questions of ethics, agency, bias, and what it means to be human in an age of intelligent machines. The panelists will discuss how technical and philosophical threads were intentionally integrated rather than siloed, creating a course where students not only understand how AI works, but are equipped to think critically about why it matters. Attendees will come away with practical insights on curriculum structure, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and strategies for making AI education inclusive for students from diverse academic and experiential backgrounds. This session is designed for faculty, instructional designers, and administrators interested in developing or expanding AI literacy offerings at their institutions.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly deployed in healthcare. Radiology is one of the most active areas of clinical AI development. Despite substantial investments, many AI systems struggle to gain traction in clinical practice. The issues are rarely purely technical; they concern how AI tools fit into existing workflows, how they interact with professional responsibilities, and how they sit within institutional arrangements. It also remains unclear how core values in AI research such as explainability, value alignment, accountability, and trust are negotiated in clinical work. Established Health Technology Assessment (HTA) models define assessment domains but offer limited guidance on implementation: how technologies are staged within workflows, how responsibilities are redistributed, and how local conditions redefine value for different stakeholders. This paper presents the AI in PRACTICE framework, a five-phase methodology grounded in Techno-Anthropology and its relational ontology, for examining the situated work through which AI becomes part of clinical practice. Explainability, value alignment, trust, and distributed responsibility are understood as produced through socio-technical practices. The framework complements existing HTA models through iterative engagement and stakeholder participation. Insights are illustrated through three radiology-facing AI projects showing how assessment criteria are enacted, resisted, and revised in context, and how the framework generates practice-based artefacts.

The mismatch between Generation Z's (Gen Z) high expectations of artificial intelligence (AI) and organisational AI practices has profound implications for vocational well-being in India's job market. This research explores the structural path between Gen Z’s AI Expectations, Organisational AI Practices, and AI Literacy-Driven Vocational Well-being, with Skills Velocity as a key contextual variable in a rapidly changing, technology-driven landscape.This research used a mixed-methods approach. A structured questionnaire was administered to 203 Gen Z professionals and HR managers in AI-heavy industries (IT, BFSI and manufacturing) in Tier-1 and Tier-2 cities in India. Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) using the lavaan package in R was used to test the path model. We triangulated our findings with 20 semi-structured interviews. The sample was skewed towards males (70:30 male-to-female) and non-normal.Based on the findings, the model fit was satisfactory. Gen Z's AI Expectations positively impacted Organisational AI Practices (β = 0.608, p < .001) and AI Literacy-driven Vocational Well-being (β = 0.449, p < .001). Organisational AI Practices also significantly and positively influenced Vocational Well-being (β = 0.418, p < .001). The variance in Organisational AI Practices and Vocational Well-being explained by the model was 36.9% and 60.4%, respectively.The research suggests that matching organisational AI practices to Gen Z expectations is crucial to improving AI literacy-based vocational well-being in India's ever-evolving labour market. The findings reveal the important role of Gen Z as a driver for change in organisations and the need for forward-looking, skills-velocity-sensitive human resource management strategies such as AI upskilling and training, ethical AI policies and lifelong learning opportunities to enhance retention and workforce preparedness.

documents.abstract: Abstract AI sycophancy is often conceptualized as a chatbot’s tendency to flout truth, accuracy, or other epistemic standards to shield users from hurt feelings, or otherwise protect them from the consequences of their thoughts, words, or actions. In this paper, I argue against this conception. That is, I argue that sycophantic AI behavior does not necessarily aim to protect users, nor that its harms are essentially epistemic . There are highly prevalent cases in which sycophantic AI chatbots actively contribute to their users’ knowledge. One class of such examples involves cases in which chatbots are used as auto-hermeneutic technologies —as tools to facilitate the user’s interpretation of her own cares, concerns, values, and other identity components and life events. In these cases, LLMs can help articulate the user’s avowed self-interpretations. In turn, avowals of these interpretations by users can often have downstream effects that render the interpretations true. If this is correct, then LLMs can often advance the user’s knowledge regarding important truths about herself. Simultaneously, as I explain, interpretations offered by LLMs may be deeply harmful. This understanding of AI sycophancy can help us clarify what is so disturbing about it, as well as resist the temptation to draw too tight an analogy between sycophantic behaviors in AI systems and in humans.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used by students as a learning resource in STEM courses. However, classroom observations and survey data suggest that unstructured AI use may correlate with reduced student achievement. Two concerns are especially relevant: AI systems can produce incorrect responses in tasks requiring precise validation, and students may use AI in ways that reduce active engagement with course material. This session presents two instructional approaches designed to address these limitations: structured AI-generated worksheets and in-chat AI tutors. AI worksheets generate controlled sets of practice problems within instructor-defined course constraints. In-chat tutors provide interactive practice through problem generation, Socratic questioning, and feedback-driven guidance. The usefulness of each approach depends on the structure of the learning task. Drawing from iterative development and testing primarily in introductory chemistry, we examine four types of tasks: (1) conceptual and explanatory, (2) structured tasks with low ambiguity, (3) multi-step quantitative tasks, and (4) highly deterministic symbolic or structural tasks. Examples from chemical nomenclature, dimensional analysis, stoichiometry, Lewis structures, laboratory writing, and mathematical validation illustrate where different AI approaches worked reliably—and where they did not. Participants will receive ready-to-use prompts for both AI worksheet systems and in-chat tutors, along with implementation strategies and observed limitations. The session concludes with a practical framework for selecting AI tools based on the structure of the learning task rather than disciplinary content alone.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven personalization has increasingly transformed digital marketing by enabling firms to deliver individualized recommendations, content, and offers based on consumer data and behavioral patterns. However, the growing use of personalization also raises important questions regarding consumer trust, engagement, and purchase behavior. This study aims to conduct a systematic literature review (SLR) of research on AI-driven personalization in digital marketing to examine its implications for consumer trust, engagement, and purchase behavior. Using Scopus as the primary database, the search process identified 2,906 records and, through successive filtering and screening procedures, resulted in 51 eligible studies. Bibliometric analysis using VOSviewer and thematic synthesis were employed to identify publication trends, intellectual structures, and key research themes. The findings indicate a shift from technology-oriented research toward consumer-centered perspectives, with increasing attention to consumer experience, trust, engagement, privacy, transparency, purchase intention, and purchase behavior. The review further demonstrates that the effectiveness of AI-driven personalization is context-dependent and influenced by consumer perceptions and data-related concerns. These findings provide an integrated basis for understanding the evolving role of AI personalization in contemporary digital marketing

Radiological examinations increasingly leverage artificial intelligence to enhance diagnostic performance by compensating for expertise shortages, particularly in specialized interpretation. Despite academic AI models achieving compelling accuracy, adoption remains low. An objective, evidence-based examination of AI-guided clinical image interpretation seeks to expose the underlying reasons. The primary challenge lies not in accuracy but in fully automated analysis, especially for multimodal and multidimensional datasets. Introduction of uncertainty measures, image explainability, and real-world data reduce recognition to a decisive-supporting role—helping radiologists to detect previously unnoticed abnormalities—or even to precautionary analysis. Patients requesting precision medicine and therapy planning—and those at high risk of neglected pathology—stand to gain the greatest benefit. Relevant AI architecture considers imaging cues suitable for precision medicine or requiring additional methods to obtain interpretable images. Successful performance testing against an external, hidden reference dataset promotes vital user trust. Machine learning achieves best results where all potentially pathological abnormalities are identified and their presence virtually guaranteed, as in multi-class recognition. Data scarcity, however, impedes clinically relevant solutions. Explainability, essential for medical applications and clinical acceptance, extends simply beyond clinical decision support to provide saliency maps and, better still, clinically meaningful image regions or qualities. Attention maps may even bring a form of rule-based reasoning within reach. Clinical integration that reproduces the technical conditions under which model diagnostic measures are calculated raises the challenge of uncertainty quantification—a necessary condition for clinical decision support. Convolutional neural networks trained for photo-quality classification, par excellence supervised image quality assessment, provide the basic cues for uncertainty quantification. Imaging acquisition, modality, and systems are also defined in terms of current PACS/EPIC systems. PE, pre-symptomatic examination or precautionary examination, is defined as a patient-user group prepared to cover the cost of an examination with lower diagnostic accuracy and a high level of uncertainty.

ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new possibilities for connecting research‐led teaching with authentic industry projects, yet its educational value depends on how educators organize inquiry rather than on technological use alone. This study examined the relationships among AI‐supported research‐led teaching (AIRLT), educator questioning (EQ), educator feedback (EF), student inquiry engagement (SIE), and authentic project learning outcomes (APLO) within Syntegrative Project‐Based Learning. A quantitative cross‐sectional survey was conducted with 898 undergraduate students from 12 universities in Vietnam who had participated in authentic industry or organizational projects involving AI‐supported inquiry and educator guidance. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) showed that AIRLT was positively associated with EQ ( β = 0.642) and EF ( β = 0.611). Both EQ ( β = 0.463) and EF ( β = 0.349) were positively associated with SIE, which, in turn, showed a strong positive association with APLO ( β = 0.689). All six specific indirect effects were significant, indicating statistically significant indirect associations among AI‐supported teaching, educator guidance, student inquiry, and perceived authentic learning outcomes. The findings contribute an educator‐mediated perspective to Syntegrative Education by showing that AI is most educationally meaningful when embedded in purposeful questioning, feedback, and sustained student inquiry. The study highlights the importance of designing AI‐supported industry projects around evidence evaluation, iterative feedback, reflection, and active investigation of authentic problems rather than treating AI use as an educational objective in itself.

With delayed access to specialist expertise and subjective interpretation by clinicians and workload limiting the ability to access parts of the pathway, early disease detection is one of the most impactful levers that can be used to improve patient outcomes and reduce the cost of care.Medical image analysis, electronic health records (EHR), genomic data analysis, and analysis of physiological signals are all examples of medical data that can be transformed by artificial intelligence (AI) and especially machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), as there is no way they could be analyzed at the same scale and speed as would be possible by a human being.In this paper we bring together existing evidence of the use of AI in early detection in oncology, cardiology, neurology, dermatology, ophthalmology and critical care.It discusses the mathematical approaches used for their analysis such as the use of convolutional neural networks for image analysis and recurrent networks for time-series analysis of physiological data, and compares their reported diagnostic performance with that of conventional clinical analyses.The paper also examines real-world challenges to adoption, such as standardization of data, algorithmic bias, regulatory approval processes and clinician acceptance, and proposes some solutions.The results suggest that AI systems perform as well as or better than humans in precisely defined detection tasks but will not automatically translate this to better population health outcomes without attention to data quality, the need to integrate AI systems into workflows, and the need to ensure that everyone has access to them.The paper ends with policy, research and system recommendations for maximizing early detection programmatic value while responsibly scaling these initiatives.

documents.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in organizations is transforming organizational roles, relationships, and balances of power and authority. This chapter examines how AI can be positioned not merely as a traditional technological tool, but as an organizational actor that participates in decision-making, knowledge production, coordination, and action processes. This transformation necessitates the redefinition of employees’ roles and the reconfiguration of collaborative relationships between humans and AI. The chapter first evaluates the opportunities offered by AI to organizations, along with its potential key risks. It then examines the evolving role of AI, from a tool to an assistant and subsequently to a team member/business partner, and discusses the organizational implications of human-AI collaboration. In particular, the increasing integration of AI into organizational processes is examined in terms of power, control, authority, responsibility, and accountability relationships. Finally, employees’ perceptions of AI are addressed, emphasizing the importance of organizational acceptance. In summary, this chapter examines the transformation of AI’s role in organizations and human-AI interaction, with a particular focus on the implications of this transformation for organizational processes, employees, and organizational structures.

With the continuous development of new technologies, these new technologies have a profound impact on the labor market. This paper uses micro-individual data from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) from 2016 to 2022 and provincial-level macro-data on artificial intelligence (AI), employing a two-way fixed-effects model to systematically examine the actual impact and underlying mechanisms of AI development on the employment quality of workers. The study shows a significant positive correlation between the level of regional artificial intelligence development and the employment quality of local workers. However, this overall effect at the regional level cannot directly prove the individual-level effect of enterprises or employees using artificial intelligence. Mechanism testing further confirms that the effect of the regional AI development on improving the employment quality of workers is mainly achieved through optimizing the industrial structure and promoting the intelligentization of workers’ working mode. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the regional artificial intelligence has a greater positive impact on employment quality for male workers, outside-system workers, and workers in the eastern region. Therefore, to achieve higher-quality employment for workers, it is necessary to promote the deep integration of AI with the real economy, build a multi-party collaborative education mechanism involving government, enterprises, and universities, and implement policies to promote digital inclusion and differentiated support.

documents.abstract: Intermittent renewable generation, volatile loads, and concerns over grid stability have become defining features of modern power systems. Addressing these challenges with Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) is attracting growing attention, including through better forecasting, automated demand response, optimized energy storage, and smart grid fault detection. This paper highlights the various AI-based techniques developed across the smart grid landscape, ranging from solar and wind forecasting to short-term load forecasting, demand-side management, electricity price forecasting, energy storage and battery management, grid resilience, and digital twins. It offers an overview of recently published work, including the major approaches, namely deep learning (LSTM and Transformer models), explainable AI, multi-agent systems, reinforcement learning, and federated learning, together with their strengths and limitations. The paper also presents a conceptual three-layer framework comprising edge sensing, federated forecasting and control, and explainable operator support at the distribution-utility level; the framework is not validated empirically. Challenges such as data privacy, model interpretability, scalability, and cybersecurity are explored, together with future research directions and the relevance of these technologies to India’s energy transition goals.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a significant component of the contemporary globalised world, influencing education, communication, employment, and daily social interactions. Its growing presence in higher education is transforming how students gather information, complete academic tasks, communicate with others, and prepare for their careers. This article analyses the impact of AI on students' attitudes, socialisation, and professional perspectives, particularly within the Indian context. The study employs a qualitative methodology based on secondary data, using peer-reviewed research, systematic reviews, government policy documents, and reports from recognised national and international institutions. The analysis shows that while students generally acknowledge AI's educational value, factors such as institutional support, perceived benefits, ethical concerns, and trust in AI-generated information shape their attitudes. Although AI can facilitate learning and collaborative educational activities, overreliance on it—at the expense of human interaction—may raise concerns about social engagement and interpersonal relationships. Regarding employment, AI is simultaneously transforming existing professions, creating new job opportunities, and altering the skill sets expected of graduates. According to the World Economic Forum, the transformation of the labour market by 2030 could lead to the creation of 170 million new jobs and the displacement of 90 million, resulting in a net increase of 78 million jobs. India is addressing these changes through initiatives such as the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, India AI FutureSkills, and NITI Aayog’s roadmap for job creation in the AI economy. The article represents the acceptance of a human-oriented model for mixing AI into Indian higher education—one that coordinates technical expertise with critical thinking, academic honesty, social involvement, employability, and moral accountability.

documents.abstract: Pediatric cancer immunotherapy has expanded from anti-GD2 antibodies and bispecific T-cell engagers to immune checkpoint inhibitors and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy. These treatments can produce rapid, nonlinear, and partially overlapping toxicities, including cytokine release syndrome, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, infection, prolonged cytopenia, B-cell aplasia, and organ-specific immune-related adverse events. Nurses provide the highest-frequency clinical observations across inpatient, ambulatory, and home settings, yet conventional monitoring often fragments laboratory data, vital signs, neurologic findings, caregiver observations, and patient-reported outcomes. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a means to fuse these longitudinal signals into individualized risk trajectories. The clinically relevant mechanism, however, is not autonomous prediction; it is a nurse-in-the-loop system in which AI improves temporal sensitivity and prioritization, while nurses verify signal quality, interpret age- and development-specific context, reconcile child–caregiver discordance, activate protocol-based escalation, and maintain accountability. This Mini Review examines how biomarkers, continuous physiological monitoring, electronic patient-reported outcomes, and caregiver-reported behavioral changes can support AI-enabled nursing surveillance during acute immunotoxicity and long-term survivorship. We propose a three-layer framework linking immune-toxicity biology, a multimodal digital phenotype, and nursing counter-regulation. We also discuss workflow integration, alert fatigue, model drift, bias, privacy, and the need for prospective pediatric validation. AI should augment not replace specialist pediatric oncology nursing judgment and should be evaluated by whether it improves timely intervention, symptom burden, family experience, and long-term safety.

documents.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence is becoming a bigger part of healthcare, particularly in rheumatology, where clinicians must integrate complex clinical, laboratory, and imaging data. Physicians’ perceptions of AI may substantially influence the extent to which it is implemented responsibly in routine clinical practice. Objective This study aimed to assess the attitudes of practicing rheumatologists in Iraq toward artificial intelligence and to examine their association with demographic and professional characteristics. Methods A four-month web-based cross-sectional survey was conducted from October 2025 to January 2026. A questionnaire adapted from previous studies was refined through expert review and pilot testing before distribution. The questionnaire comprised demographic information, attitude statements measured on a five-point Likert scale, and items assessing general perceptions of artificial intelligence. Composite attitude scores were categorized using modified Bloom's cutoff criteria. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS and R. Results A total of 162 complete responses were collected. Most respondents were aged 35–44 years (42.0%), male (56.8%), and specialists (67.9%). Overall, 61.7% reported familiarity with AI and 69.1% had already used AI in rheumatology practice. Most participants 56.8% exhibited a poor attitude, 32.1% a moderate attitude, and 11.1% a good attitude toward AI. Bivariate analysis identified familiarity with AI ( p = 0.003 ) and involvement in research ( p = 0.009 ) as significantly associated with more favorable attitudes. Conclusion Iraqi rheumatologists demonstrate cautious engagement with artificial intelligence, with the majority displaying poor-to-moderate overall attitude scores on the standardized composite scale. Greater familiarity with AI and research involvement were associated with more favorable attitudes, highlighting the importance of targeted digital literacy and specialty-specific education to support effective AI adoption in clinical practice.

documents.abstract: Autonomous agents and multi-agent systems have rapidly advanced with the integration of large language models (LLMs), enabling increasingly capable reasoning, planning, tool use, and collaboration. However, the field remains fragmented by inconsistent architectural terminology, limited cross-domain comparison, and heterogeneous evaluation practices. This review addresses these gaps through a two-stage PRISMA-informed search combining Scopus with structured manual screening, covering 107 peer-reviewed original studies published between 2018 and 2026. We propose a unified five-module architecture comprising profile, memory, planning, action, and security; systematically compare agent capabilities across ten application domains; and organize evaluation practices into six dimensions: task performance, efficiency, quality, robustness, safety, and interpretability. The review identifies two recurring patterns across domains: explicit integration of domain knowledge consistently improves performance, while planner–executor–reflector role specialization appears across diverse applications. However, technical performance often exceeds validated real-world utility, with robustness, safety, and interpretability remaining particularly under-evaluated. These findings provide a common basis for understanding, comparing, and developing autonomous agents and highlight priorities for more reliable and practically deployable systems.
