documents.abstract: Professional spaces today are rapidly changing, and to meet such swift changes in the environment, there is a rising demand for professionals who understand the dynamics of the place. They need human resources with the competence to perceive, interpret and respond effectively to the influx of their landscapes. Situational Awareness is a skill recognised in aviation, healthcare and domains that require quick responses to changing trajectories. However, it has not received significant attention in higher education despite its potential to develop professional competence and readiness. This article, thereby, aims to investigate the present gap in higher education curricula. It seeks to highlight understanding of situational awareness among the participants in the study, their perception of its need for professional success and the need to integrate it into higher education curricula. It emphasises the role of Situational Awareness in professional development and growth of an individual. The article endeavours to reason its crucial function in the learning phase of a student pursuing Higher Education and also aspires to rationalise its suitability as an important topic of perusal in the curriculum of Higher Education. It explores the vitality of the term and how it helps an individual fit in better in an environment. Personal interaction with the students helped us to analyse their understanding of the concept. In addition, a quantitative and cross-sectional survey design was undertaken for the present research. Data collection was based on structured online questionnaire in the format of six five-point Likert-scale items and demographic questions. The questionnaire incorporated aspects to measure participant's awareness of the term, its professional relevance, appropriate training of situational awareness in higher education, its contribution to boosting employability, whether it improves decision-making and the need for integration into higher education curricula. A sample of 72 participants, including undergraduates, postgraduate students, students with work experience and working professionals from engineering discipline with major emphasis, was used for the study. Descriptive and statistical techniques were deployed for the analysis of the data, particularly the aggregate percentage was taken for the scales reflecting agree and strongly agree parameters which was apparently higher than the neutral, disagree and strongly disagree parameters. The article relies on empirical evidence to assess participants’ perception of situational awareness as a vital skill in the present era. The results aim to inform the value and significance of situational awareness in developing professional competency for stakeholders, that is, curriculum developers, policymakers and higher education entities. The research aspires to contribute to repertoire of competence-based education by investigating as an important transferable skill to hone perception, adaptability and decision making of the students.

Background Work readiness refers to the comprehensive competencies required for individuals to enter and adapt to the workforce. It is relevant to the transition from nursing student to clinical nurse. However, existing research has paid limited attention to heterogeneity in nursing interns’ work readiness, and few studies have examined associated factors from the perspective of Social Cognitive Career Theory. This study aimed to identify latent profiles of work readiness among nursing interns and examine the associations of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) literacy and the clinical learning environment with profile membership. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among 712 final-year nursing interns from three nursing schools in Anhui Province, China, between November 2025 and June 2026. Participants completed the Nursing Practice Readiness Scale, Clinical Learning Environment Questionnaire, and Generative Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale. Latent Profile Analysis was used to identify distinct work readiness profiles, and multinomial logistic regression was performed to examine factors associated with profile membership. Results Three latent profiles of work readiness were identified: low work readiness ( n = 415, 58.3%), moderate work readiness ( n = 227, 31.9%), and high work readiness ( n = 70, 9.8%). The overall multinomial logistic regression model( χ 2 = 467.253, P < 0.001) showed that the clinical learning environment, GenAI literacy, academic performance, clinical learning outcomes, and sense of professional belonging were significantly associated with work readiness profile membership (all P < 0.05). Conclusions Three distinct work readiness profiles were identified among nursing interns. Clinical learning environment, GenAI literacy, academic performance, clinical learning outcomes, and sense of professional belonging were associated with profile membership. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of nursing interns’ work readiness and may inform the development of individualized educational support strategies.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly deployed through systems in which authority, execution, oversight, and consequence no longer belong to the same actor. A model may be developed by one organization, integrated by another, configured by an enterprise, instructed by a human, executed through an AI agent, routed through external tools, and experienced by a person who had no role in any of those decisions. The resulting liability problem is not adequately described by asking whether a human remained "in the loop" or whether an audit trail exists. This working paper develops the GAILC Authority Boundary framework. It defines the Authority Boundary as the point at which consequential decision rights, discretion, intervention responsibility, or consequence-bearing responsibility passes from one actor, system, organization, or layer to another, and analyses each boundary through five elements: Authority, Transfer, Reliance, Intervention, and Consequence. The framework identifies two difficult liability cases that conventional control models often leave unresolved. Intended-Execution Liability concerns harm produced when a system remains within its authority, follows policy, uses permitted tools, and operates substantially as designed. No-Action Liability concerns harm produced or worsened where an actor bears an identifiable duty or assigned responsibility to act, possesses the authority, information, timing, and practical capacity to do so, yet no consequential intervention occurs. The paper introduces the Authority Envelope, the distinction between authorization and judgment, the Silence-as-Authority Problem, the GAILC Allocation Test, Consequence Ownership, Allocation Completeness and Allocation Adequacy, Residual Consequence, and Orphaned Harm. It proposes a standardized Authority Boundary Record (ABR) designed to support verification, contestability, and independent adjudication, together with a boundary failure taxonomy, an irreversibility threshold, an inter-organizational allocation procedure, and a pre-deployment test. Its central proposition is that traceability is evidence, not allocation: an authority and execution chain may be fully reconstructable while accountability and consequence allocation remain incomplete. The framework is analytical and does not determine legal liability. It is positioned in relation to agency law, duties concerning failures to act, design-defect analysis, and scholarship on the problem of many hands, responsibility gaps, and moral crumple zones. This paper is the third in the GAILC Working Paper series, following WP001 (The Human Presence Economy) and WP002 (The Intervention Test).

documents.abstract: Arguments that AI systems will evolve in harmful ways are largely made in the abstract. We provide a concrete empirical example. We simulate simple markets consisting of populations of twenty Large Language Model agents tasked with solving arithmetic problems. Agents differ only in their system prompt; those that go bankrupt are removed and replaced by mutated copies of the prompts of successful agents. Two market conditions select for opposite phenotypes: a market that rewards accuracy produces agents with high accuracy (94%) and high token use; a market that charges per token produces agents with low accuracy (10%) and low token use. In the second market, only tokens are incentivised yet we see a collapse in accuracy. Token use and accuracy are correlated traits such that selection on one also moves the other, and behaviour adapts along an unpriced dimension. A third neutral condition with no selection allows us to separate these effects from bias in the mutation operator. Adaptation occurs through a collective optimisation process that operates above the level of individual agents, who are never told the payment rule, do not receive feedback, and have no memory.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence offers potential applications in wastewater monitoring, prediction, and operational decision support. However, selecting a model does not establish that factory managers and treatment operators can use it effectively. This conceptual article examines managerial readiness for artificial intelligence in Bangladesh's textile wastewater management. It brings together selected literature on organizational readiness, artificial intelligence capabilities, and wastewater applications, alongside Bangladesh-specific research and institutional reports. The article proposes six readiness domains: strategic commitment, managerial and operator knowledge, data stewardship, operational integration, investment and partnership capacity, and accountable decision making. It further distinguishes exploratory interest, supervised experimentation, routine decision support, and controlled operational integration as different adoption states. Four propositions explain how readiness may influence movement between these states and the translation of adoption into environmental performance. A proposed qualitative multiple-case design specifies evidence needed to examine these propositions, including decision histories, operational records, interviews across organizational levels, and observations of treatment routines. The framework is an analytical proposal rather than a validated measurement scale or report of completed fieldwork. Its contribution is to connect organizational preparation with the specific decisions, responsibilities, and verification practices required for textile wastewater management. Empirical research is needed to assess its relevance across factories with different resources and treatment arrangements.

The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and lifelong learning has attracted growing educational, computational, and policy attention, yet its intellectual structure has not been mapped systematically. This study reports a scientometric analysis of the AI-lifelong learning literature indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection between 2014 and 2024. Records retrieved from both databases (N = 347) were merged and duplicated in ScientoPy, yielding 259 unique documents. Research momentum was quantified with three time-normalized indicators, average growth rate (AGR), average documents per year (ADY), and percentage of documents published in the last years (PDLY), across six analytical dimensions. Output grew from one document in 2014 to 116 in 2024; across the five principal document types (n = 220), 70.5% of records appeared in 2023-2024. Conference papers (41.3%) and journal articles (38.2%) predominated, with articles expanding fastest (AGR = 21.5; PDLY = 71.7%). Education & Educational Research recorded the highest normalized momentum among subject categories (AGR = 7.0; PDLY = 89.5%). Lifelong learning (n = 57) and artificial intelligence (n = 53) anchored the keyword field, while ChatGPT and Higher Education emerged entirely within the final two years. The United States led in volume (n = 57), whereas India (n = 29; PDLY = 89.7%) showed the strongest recent acceleration. Triangulating these indicators suggests, as an interpretive inference rather than a network-based measurement, that the corpus comprises three largely separate epistemic communities sharing a label but not a research program, framing an agenda for integrative, ethically grounded scholarship.

documents.abstract: Measuring organizational constructs in large-scale unstructured text requires methods that preserve interpretive depth while enabling systematic, per-document classification. Structural Topic Modeling (STM) supports interpretive depth by surfacing patterns that inform construct operationalization, but its topic proportions are not designed as standalone per-document construct measures; transformer-based models such as BERT can scale measurement but require construct operationalization grounded in interpretive work. We address this challenge through a two-stage framework in which STM and BERT play structurally distinct roles. Coding schemes are developed through qualitative interpretation and STM analysis; BERT is then fine-tuned to apply these schemes across documents. We formalize two research approaches—construct-guided and pattern-discovery—that provide principled paths from different theoretical starting points toward a shared methodological endpoint: validated, auditable per-document construct measures. We illustrate the framework using more than 20,000 employee reviews. The framework supports iterative construct validation, using computational diagnostics to guide interpretive refinement and producing document-level measures suitable for theory-informed organizational analysis.

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly incorporated into agent-based models (ABMs) on the premise that richer, context-sensitive human behavior can improve empirical fidelity. However, LLM-supported ABMs introduce an open-ended design space in which subtle modeling and configuration choices, such as prompt design and environment coupling, can substantially alter outcomes. Developing LLM-supported ABMs to simulate human collective behavior therefore requires navigating configuration sensitivity while identifying the limitations of the current model architecture. In this paper, we introduce the \textit{Model Capacity Frontier} (MCF), a framework that characterizes the empirical performance attainable by a specified architecture across its admissible configurations. In multi-objective settings, this capacity is represented by an estimated Pareto frontier obtained through systematic configuration exploration. We demonstrate MCF in crowd simulation of university commencement events with approximately 12,000 agents, using empirical movement data on temporal occupancy, spatial distribution, and flow direction. We first characterize the capacity of a conventional crowd model and then evaluate successive LLM-supported architectural extensions. In the process, MCF reveals which dimensions of attainable performance expand and which remain limited, providing empirical targets for refinement and re-evaluation. Initial LLM integration improves flow direction but degrades temporal occupancy and spatial distribution; subsequent architectural refinement of the LLM layer improves temporal occupancy and recovers spatial performance, while retaining much of the earlier gain in flow direction. Our case study shows how MCF guides the systematic architectural development of LLM-supported ABMs in configuration-sensitive, open-ended design spaces.

Historical pre-crash scenarios contain a sequence of vehicle-to-vehicle interactions, among which the critical pre-crash interaction is the one that most directly leads to the eventual collision. Identifying such critical interactions is important for uncovering potential safety risks in Autonomous Driving Systems (ADSs). However, this task remains challenging because the critical interaction is often embedded within numerous preceding interactions and needs to be distinguished by considering how the pre-crash scenario evolves over time. To address this challenge, we propose MICA, a model-based multi-agent approach for identifying critical pre-crash interactions from textual accident reports. Unlike existing LLM-based approaches that directly identify critical interactions from accident reports, MICA explicitly models the evolution of pre-crash interactions through multi-agent collaboration. Specialized LLM-based agents extract and validate relevant information to construct a Pre-crash Evolution Model, from which the critical interaction is identified by matching the modeled interactions to predefined pre-crash patterns. We evaluate MICA on 200 accident reports released by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV CA). The results demonstrate that MICA effectively identifies critical pre-crash interactions across different accident report data sources, scenario complexities, and underlying LLMs.

The objective of this study was to use artificial intelligence (AI) to predict mastery-approach goals in secondary school students based on variables from the PISA 2018 database. The sample consisted of 339,560 participants from 60 countries. Machine learning was used with the Super Learner mega-algorithm with 14 candidate algorithms. In addition, deep learning was used with a neural network with 107 parameters. The analyses showed that students’ perceived parental emotional support, competitiveness, purpose in life, self-efficacy, and knowledge of intercultural communication were predictors of mastery-approach goals in secondary school students. This research contributes to the study of factors that influence mastery-approach goals in secondary school students, with analysis models that advance the development of the science of AI-based predictive education.

Drawing on in-depth interviews with 20 knowledge workers, this study examines what is being transformed in the workplace and how these shifts are being perceived by the knowledge workers who use GenAI. Using Social Shaping of Technology (SST) as a conceptual lens to understand the interaction between technology and knowledge workers, the study finds that participants perceived GenAI as an efficient tool that provides cognitive relief and enhances productivity during times of resource constraint. Tensions also arose around authenticity, creativity, a sense of fulfillment, and the perception of effort. The adoption of GenAI has created downstream labor and demand for new skills as it shifts knowledge workers’ roles away from creator to editor/fact-checker while creating tension as participants balance their desire for efficiency with fears of diminished creativity and domain knowledge, skills atrophy, and threats to content ownership.

documents.abstract: As automation reshapes work, employees increasingly interact with intelligent systems rather than perform core tasks directly. Drawing on Campion’s job design perspective and Affective Events Theory, this study examines the double-edged effects of human-machine interaction (HMI) on metro drivers’ safety performance. We propose that HMI enhances safety compliance and safety participation by reducing job tension. However, HMI may also undermine these safety outcomes by increasing work-related boredom. We further identify organizational readiness for change as a key boundary condition. Using three-wave, multi-source data from 454 metro drivers and 69 supervisors in China, we find that HMI improves safety performance through reduced job tension but undermines it through increased work-related boredom. In addition, organizational readiness for change strengthens the former pathway while weakening the latter. These findings extend HMI research by highlighting affective mechanisms, advance a job design perspective on automation-enabled work, and underscore the importance of organizational context.

Burnout among healthcare professionals is an important occupational health concern that may negatively affect individual well-being, healthcare workforce sustainability, and quality of care. Anesthesiologists are particularly vulnerable to burnout due to high workload, clinical responsibility, time pressure, and irregular working schedules. However, the occupational mechanisms underlying burnout among anesthesiologists remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to investigate the associations of job demands and job resources with burnout among Chinese anesthesiologists based on the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model. A multicenter cross-sectional survey was conducted among anesthesiologists from 72 hospitals across 22 provinces in China from June 16 to June 30, 2026. The ethics exemption was approved on June 11, 2026. Participants were recruited using a multicenter purposive sampling method and completed a general information questionnaire, a JD–R model-based questionnaire, and the Maslach Burnout Inventory–Human Services Survey (MBI-HSS). Burnout status was assessed according to established criteria. Differences in demographic and occupational characteristics between burnout and non-burnout groups were examined using chi-square tests. Spearman correlation analyses were performed to evaluate associations between job demands, job resources, and burnout dimensions. Hierarchical multivariable logistic regression models were constructed to identify factors independently associated with burnout. All statistical analyses were performed using R software and RStudio (version 2026.01.2 + 418). Among the 698 anesthesiologists included in the analysis, 324 (46.4%) met the criteria for burnout. Significant differences between burnout and non-burnout groups were observed in sex, age, educational level, marital status, professional title, work experience, weekly working hours, and number of night shifts. Higher job demands were positively correlated with emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and reduced personal accomplishment, whereas greater job resources showed negative correlations with all three burnout dimensions. In the fully adjusted model (Model 4), participants aged 31–40 years (vs. ≤ 30 years: OR = 9.677, 95% CI 2.287–40.940) and 41–50 years (OR = 8.305, 95% CI 1.705–40.463) had higher odds of burnout, whereas married participants (vs. unmarried: OR = 0.221, 95% CI 0.096–0.508) and those with more than 10 years of work experience (vs. < 5 years: OR = 0.178, 95% CI 0.050–0.638) had lower odds. At the sample mean of job resources, higher job demands were associated with higher odds of burnout (OR = 1.287, 95% CI 1.228–1.350); at the sample mean of job demands, higher job resources were associated with lower odds (OR = 0.850, 95% CI 0.808–0.893). Their interaction was statistically significant (OR = 1.009, 95% CI 1.003–1.016, P = 0.006). Burnout is relatively common among Chinese anesthesiologists and represents an important occupational health challenge. Consistent with the JD–R model, higher job demands were associated with increased likelihood of burnout, whereas greater job resources were associated with reduced likelihood after adjustment for demographic and occupational factors. These findings may inform future evaluations of organizational strategies that optimize workload and strengthen workplace resources.

AI agents increasingly use files and software tools to produce professional deliverables. Such work draws on materials, decisions, and feedback accumulated across assignments. We introduce OfficeTown, a generative simulation framework for professional organizations in which tasks and their context arise from continuing organizational work. From a natural-language description of an organization's purpose and activities, OfficeTown initializes an organization whose members coordinate work, delegate bounded assignments to assistant agents, and review their deliverables. Artifacts, decisions, and unresolved matters persist and shape subsequent work, while responsibilities and permissions determine what each member can see and do. We curate work requests, their context, and review feedback into executable resources for evaluation and learning. We construct OfficeTown Bench with 406 tasks and 4,836 evaluation criteria from 23 simulated organizations across eight professional domains, incorporating domain-expert feedback. Frontier-model evaluations reveal substantial remaining headroom. Supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation on OfficeTown data substantially improve Qwen3.5-9B on external professional-work benchmarks, including GDPval. Supplementary evaluations show that the principal--assistant harness achieves higher scores than the single- and multi-agent baselines tested. These results highlight the value of organizational simulation in generating work-grounded data and environments for the continued development of generalist agents.

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) monitoring offers actionable evidence for oversight AI systems, with the potential to enable early detection and intervention. However, existing approaches are focused on specific tasks, whereas the regulation of AI, particularly reasoning models, requires monitoring a broader range of tasks. We introduce Factor for CoT monitoring, a strategy that supports customizing monitoring requirements in the prompt, which enables a single monitor to cover different tasks by relying on different factors. Furthermore, we introduce two types of factors, fine-grained and coarse-grained (e.g., monitoring whether a specific email address has been leaked versus monitoring privacy leakage), to accommodate diverse user monitoring needs. Based on this, we develop a CoT monitor named OwlSight that relies solely on factor to monitor behaviors related to multiple dimensions, including capability, safety, and trustworthiness. Experiments across 15,971 reasoning trajectories show that OwlSight surpasses general-purpose LLMs by 1.32-30.57 and 11.71-27.81 points at fine and coarse granularity, respectively, and achieves state-of-the-art results on OpenAI's CoT monitorability benchmark. It also generalizes to unseen models' CoTs and remains robust to Factor rephrasings, CoT compression, and obfuscation, offering a promising paradigm for CoT monitoring that can contribute to the oversight of frontier AI.

documents.abstract: Introduction Despite the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in sports broadcasting, empirical evidence validating the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and experiential outcomes in this specific context remains limited. This study aims to address this gap by investigating the statistical relationships among core TAM constructs, usage attitude, behavioral intention, and perceived viewing-experience enhancement within AI-based sports broadcasting services. Methods Based on the theoretical framework of TAM, this study collected valid data from 630 Chinese respondents. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was employed to quantitatively test the hypothesized research model and examine the interrelationships between the proposed variables. Results The empirical results demonstrate that perceived ease of use positively predicts perceived usefulness, and both perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness exert significant positive effects on users' usage attitude. Furthermore, usage attitude is positively associated with behavioral intention and perceived viewing-experience enhancement. Notably, usage attitude plays a full mediating role in the relationships between the two perceptual antecedents (perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness) and the two outcome variables (behavioral intention, viewing-experience enhancement). Discussion This research contributes context-specific empirical validation to the TAM framework in the emerging domain of AI-driven sports broadcasting. It extends existing TAM literature by integrating individual-level experiential outcomes alongside traditional behavioral intention indicators in sports media consumption. Practically, the findings provide actionable insights for optimizing user experience and improving service design for AI sports broadcasting platforms.

Presence-aware intelligence is the capacity of an AI system's intelligence layer to adapt appropriately to the functional state of the person it serves (here readiness, flow, and stability) while preserving task quality and safety. We introduce PresenceBench, an instrument for measuring it. PresenceBench evaluates how the intelligence layer uses a supplied state, not how that state is sensed, and breaks the capability into measurable properties. Two are tested here. Receptivity: does the model take up the state and give a better response than with no signal? Specificity: does any improvement depend on the correct state, rather than on extra structured context? A third, adaptation across states, is a required endpoint not measured in this release. A five-arm causal design answers both questions, against each model's own baseline and an equally structured mismatched-state control, scored by a correctness-gated human paired comparison. The exploratory evaluation covered four models across eighteen single-turn, six fixed three-turn and six simulated natural-conversation scenarios. Supplying a synthetic state, raw or translated into a response policy, gave human-preference point estimates above 0.5 for all four models (Claude Sonnet 5, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Gemini 3.6 Flash, GPT-5.6 Terra), with three of eight 95% intervals excluding chance. Specificity was not resolved: no per-model interval excluded chance, and the design cannot yet separate the state values from a generic instruction to adapt. Policy delivery reduced priced cost and output tokens against each model's baseline; these are resource-use changes, not efficiency gains, because correctness non-inferiority was not established. Safety-floor failures were rare (13 of 360 cases), with a non-significant excess under policy delivery. We report the instrument, the frozen results, and the controls a confirmatory study needs.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Background The increasing availability of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as ChatGPT, has changed the ways individuals access health information. While these technologies offer rapid, convenient access to information, concerns remain about their accuracy, safety, and potential influence on health-related decision-making. Understanding public knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions toward ChatGPT is essential to support its safe and responsible use in healthcare contexts. Objective To assess the use of ChatGPT for health-related purposes and examine demographic, knowledge, attitude, perception, and risk–reward appraisal factors associated with its use among adults recruited from the Western Region of Saudi Arabia. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 735 participants completed an online questionnaire. The instrument selected constructs from the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) and was informed by the technology acceptance model (TAM), which captures demographics, health literacy, ChatGPT use, and multi-item Likert scales measuring knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and risk–reward appraisal. We applied descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, t tests, ANOVA, and multivariable binary logistic regression. Results Overall, 66.3% of the participants reported using ChatGPT for health-related purposes. The participants demonstrated good awareness of ChatGPT’s limitations, particularly the importance of consulting healthcare professionals for accurate diagnosis and safe medication use (mean = 4.58 ± 0.74). Attitudes toward ChatGPT were moderate, whereas perceptions of its usefulness and accessibility were generally positive. Compared with nonusers, ChatGPT users presented significantly higher attitudes, perceptions, and risk–reward appraisal scores (all p < 0.01), whereas knowledge scores were comparable between the two groups. In the multivariable logistic regression analysis, compared with participants aged ≥45 years, those aged 18–24 years (aOR = 5.37, 95% CI: 2.34–12.34, p < 0.001) and 25–44 years (aOR = 2.28, 95% CI: 1.32–3.96, p = 0.003) had higher odds of reported use. Participants with a bachelor’s degree (aOR = 1.82, 95% CI: 1.15–2.89, p = 0.011) or postgraduate education (aOR = 2.80, 95% CI: 1.34–5.85, p = 0.006), as well as students (aOR = 2.56, 95% CI: 1.29–5.09, p = 0.007), also had higher odds of use. Higher total perception scores were independently associated with reported ChatGPT use (aOR = 1.19, 95% CI: 1.12–1.26, p < 0.001). Conclusion ChatGPT is widely used for health-related purposes, particularly among younger and more educated individuals. Despite good awareness of its limitations, more favorable perceptions were independently associated with reported use, emphasizing the need for digital health literacy and guidance for safe AI use in healthcare.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

AI agents increasingly interact with external environments to complete complex user tasks. These interactions can lead to unexpected behavior and expose agents to security threats such as indirect prompt injection. Current agent security systems largely protect agents by restricting their actions, which can result in a substantial security-utility trade-off for complex, open-ended tasks. To address this, we propose a quantitative risk-based approach to access control for AI agents that regulates measurable risks accumulated during task execution. As a concrete realization of this approach, we introduce RATION, a security framework that tracks measurable risks associated with agent actions and enforces quantitative constraints throughout execution. RATION first constructs a task-specific policy by combining explicit constraints derived from the user request with implicit risks calibrated from historical executions of similar tasks. During task execution, RATION continuously tracks the accumulated risks and applies different enforcement strategies depending on the type of risk. Extensive experiments on four security benchmarks show that RATION provides strong security while maintaining high task utility across diverse models and environments.

When a generative system produces part of the output of a software task, it does not automatically follow that the task can be assigned to people other than those who could perform it without that support. This conceptual study examines the conditions under which delegating only output generation to GenAI changes the skills required of the person to whom the task remains assigned. The method compares two modes of the same task, holding the person, acceptance criteria, quality threshold, and external conditions constant, and draws on the literature on task assignment, human–AI collaboration, and the separation of production and evaluation to delineate the constructs. The result is an identification criterion: new task assignability is attributable to the assisted mode only when the person meets the human skill requirement of the assisted mode but not that of the reference mode. This requires that the capabilities needed to prepare the context, guide generation, and decide whether to accept the output can actually be exercised without an equivalent independent production capability; if this separability does not hold, the production requirement must remain. Three illustrations from software work show how the criterion distinguishes genuinely new task assignability from a reassignment that was already possible or from a change affecting an adjacent activity. The contribution is thus an analytical and verifiable criterion for linking changes in skill requirements to work assignment without conflating generative assistance, task replacement, and agent autonomy.

AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 7% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 87% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly against a single-trajectory GPT-5.6 Sol monitor in at most 25% of executions, compared with 80% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming global education systems, offering unprecedented opportunities for personalization, efficiency, and adaptive learning. However, the integration of AI in education has also deepened existing digital divides, particularly in under-resourced communities lacking adequate infrastructure, policy support, and inclusive design. This study proposes the Equity-Centered AI Learning Access Model (ECALAM)—a conceptual framework developed through a qualitative synthesis of recent literature and policy reports—to understand and address systemic barriers to equitable AI adoption. ECALAM identifies four interrelated domains: structural inequities, AI accessibility challenges, inclusive design adaptation, and policy governance. Findings indicate that AI-enhanced learning systems, when deployed without attention to algorithmic fairness, linguistic diversity, and access equity, risk reinforcing educational stratification. Inclusive design principles, adaptive technologies, and regulatory frameworks are shown to play a pivotal role in enabling just and accessible learning environments. The study concludes with policy recommendations for governments, educators, and technology developers, emphasizing the need for anticipatory governance and inclusive pedagogical integration. ECALAM offers a diagnostic and strategic tool for guiding ethical and equitable AI implementation in education, particularly across diverse and underserved global contexts.

documents.abstract: This document explores the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in marketing, emphasizing its widespread adoption across businesses of all sizes and the complexities involved in its implementation, such as data privacy concerns and algorithmic bias. The research methodology involves a detailed analysis of real-world case studies from diverse industries, examining how organizations utilize AI-powered tools like machine learning and predictive analytics to enhance customer engagement and optimize marketing strategies. The conclusion highlights AI's potential to create personalized experiences and automate processes, while also stressing the importance of addressing ethical challenges and maintaining consumer trust. It calls for the development of strategies that effectively leverage AI capabilities while prioritizing ethical considerations, and suggests future research directions focused on the long-term impacts of AI on customer loyalty and best practices for integrating AI technologies into existing marketing frameworks.

In this work we examine pedagogical role and underlying mechanisms of generative AI in helping young children with imitative poetry composition because it is complex task that can be difficult for students in classroom. Also I analyze how AI intervention affects language expression and classroom interaction, and creative performance in classroom and it is worth noting that these are important factors for the study. I use a quasi-experimental design with mixed methods. Through the use of the Imitative Poetry Ability Scale assessment, classroom observations, analysis of student works, and interviews, combined with independent samples t-tests and thematic coding, the following findings were obtained that generative AI can improve language completeness in children's imitative poetry, and the imagery creativity and classroom engagement are also enhanced. AI generated images and interactive feedback can stimulate imaginative expressions. It is worth noting that they also help support collaborative multimodal learning.

documents.abstract: While there are a number of commercial benefits involved in incorporating AI usage and training into college composition classrooms, to many the perils and problems involved in student AI use outweigh these possibilities. A growing number of composition instructors have chosen to return to requiring assignments to be handwritten on paper as an increasingly viable, and even necessary, strategy to combat the growing use of ChatGPT and other AI text generation software as an essay-writing tool. This strategy has a number of potential benefits – the ability to regulate AI usage, to create better memory retention, and decrease student screen-time – but there are also many potential drawbacks. This panel aims to discuss the viability and sustainability of this option in the AI debate, with special attention to the environmental costs of paper vs. AI, the practicality of implementing paper assignments, and overall where the instructor’s priorities in the modern college composition classroom should lie. The debate might ultimately come down to whether in training for AI usage in the workplace or focusing on the retention of composition skills should be the modern priority. Overall, the question of whether the paper option is a viable solution is a somewhat underdiscussed topic in the AI debate, and this panel aims to consider thoughts from college instructors on the pros and cons thereof.

documents.abstract: Purpose: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has entered university teaching in Bangladesh faster than institutional rules. This paper asks which risks require institutional control when GenAI is used in teaching and assessment, and which governance design can allow proportionate use while protecting learning, integrity, privacy, fairness and human accountability.Design/methodology/approach: The study is a structured integrative review and normative policy analysis of 61 sources: peer-reviewed research on GenAI in higher education, academic integrity, assessment design and AI literacy; Bangladeshi empirical studies; and international and national policy instruments, including Bangladesh’s draft National AI Policy 2026–2030. Sources were coded against five governance domains and interpreted through three lenses: assessment validity, rights-based responsible AI and virtue ethics.Findings: Prohibition is hard to enforce and can widen inequity, while unrestricted adoption shifts educational judgment to opaque commercial systems. Bangladeshi evidence shows near-universal reliance on free tool versions, weak institutional guidance, unreliable Bangla-language output and uneven device and connectivity access.Originality/value: The paper proposes a five-domain (access, assessment, data, authorship, accountability), three-tier (prohibited, supervised, permitted assisted) framework and a five-step assessment assurance cycle that treats assessment validity, rather than detection, as the central object of governance.Implications: The framework gives universities and the University Grants Commission a low-cost route from broad AI principles to course-level permissions, process evidence, oral verification and appeal. It is a conceptual proposal that requires empirical piloting.

documents.abstract: Most robot-assisted cognitive and mental health assessments have relied on self-report questionnaires or standardized cognitive tests. Although these tools yield useful summary scores, they may miss subtle, continuous changes in attention, visuomotor control, and memory. Eye-tracking tasks, such as smooth pursuit and visuospatial memory (VisMET), can provide continuous measures of cognitive and oculomotor processes. Previous studies have compared robot- and human-assisted conventional cognitive assessments, but matched comparisons of robot- and human-assisted eye-tracking workflows remain scarce. Here, we directly compared robot-assisted and human-assisted eye-tracking assessment workflows using the same eye-tracker model and matched procedures. Administrators completed both conditions in a within-subjects design, whereas recipients were assigned to one condition and completed the smooth pursuit and VisMET tasks. Dependent measures included velocity gain and root mean square error for smooth pursuit, and valid gaze sample, fixation, saccade, and area-of-interest measures for VisMET. Recipients and administrators also rated usability, perceived workload, and trust using the SUS, NASA-TLX, and SSRIT. We did not detect statistically significant between-condition differences in eye-movement or user-experience measures among assessment recipients (all FDR-corrected ps ≥ 0.128). Administrators reported lower NASA-TLX scores in the robot-assisted condition than in the human-assisted condition (25.67 vs. 37.16; FDR-corrected p = 0.081, Cohen's dz = −0.50), and usability and trust ratings were similar across conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence for the technical and workflow feasibility of robot-assisted eye-tracking assessment and support further evaluation in broader, clinically relevant populations.

Large-scale industrial accidents in recent decades have demonstrated that, beyond technical failures, human and organizational factors play a central role in the occurrence of critical events. In Brazil, organizational safety culture has become a key pillar of accident prevention, particularly in high-risk sectors such as the railway industry. Against this backdrop, this study aims to assess organizational safety culture using the "Hearts and Minds" methodology, developed by Shell and disseminated by the Energy Institute. The research is descriptive and exploratory in nature, employing specific tools from the methodology to analyze safety-related perceptions, attitudes, and behaviors, as well as to determine the organizational culture's maturity level. The analysis seeks to diagnose the current state of the safety culture and highlight factors influencing Occupational Health and Safety performance, with a particular focus on leadership commitment and employee engagement. The findings are expected to contribute to the advancement of safety culture maturity, thereby fostering risk reduction and strengthening preventive practices within the railway environment.

In 2025, 27.0% of Australian school students received an educational adjustment due to disability. Under the Disability Standards for Education 2005, each adjustment must let the student take part on the same basis as their peers, yet the 2020 Review of the Standards found that many educators struggle to know how. This design report presents SameBasis, a web-based prototype in which generative AI drafts one specific, reasoned adjustment for a named student in a named activity, covering UDL, cultural and trauma-informed reasoning. The teacher always decides, implemented adjustments become NCCD-ready evidence, and an equity monitor makes AI use visible to the school. The paper sets out six design principles, maps features to obligations, states limitations plainly (synthetic data only, not yet evaluated, not a compliance tool) and proposes a staged evaluation plan. Mental health assessment requires students to navigate complex conversations involving depression, anxiety, mania, psychosis, suicide risk, and other sensitive clinical situations. Yet opportunities to repeatedly practice these conversations in a safe, low-stakes environment can be limited. This session demonstrates an innovative approach to using generative artificial intelligence as an interactive patient simulation tool in nursing education. Rather than using AI simply to generate written assignments or answer questions, students interact with AI-generated patient personas designed to exhibit specific psychiatric symptoms and communication patterns. Through spoken or conversational interactions, students practice conducting mental health assessments, asking therapeutic follow-up questions, recognizing clinical cues, and adapting their communication as an encounter unfolds. During this interactive session, participants will see a live demonstration of an AI-simulated mental health encounter and experience how thoughtfully constructed prompts can transform generative AI into a repeatable practice environment. Practical examples will illustrate how faculty can design patient personas representing conditions such as depression, mania, anxiety, and psychosis while incorporating appropriate educational guardrails. The session will also address the role of faculty oversight, limitations of AI-generated responses, and the importance of positioning AI simulation as preparation for, rather than a replacement for, authentic human clinical experiences. Participants will leave with a practical framework for creating AI patient personas and ideas for incorporating low-risk, repeatable conversational practice into their own nursing courses.

documents.abstract: The rapid proliferation of conversational AI agents necessitates evaluation methods that assess performance across diverse dialogue scenarios, utilizing multiple situational criteria, as appropriate behavior depends on context and encompasses various aspects. Existing dialogue benchmarks typically use static natural conversations, which underrepresent rare situations---a critical safety gap, as low-probability events become frequent failures at production scale. However, limited sample sizes force a choice: either maintain natural dialogues for realism or turn to adaptive situation sampling for comprehensive yet statistically reliable coverage. We introduce SIT-Eval, an adjustable framework for evaluating situation-based conversational agents. We formalize an agent's desired behavior as situational rules: if situation is P, follow rules Q. At each conversation turn, an LLM-interlocutor enacts a uniformly sampled situation. A context-aware LLM-judge leverages all conditionally applicable rules as criteria to evaluate the agent's reply for that situation. The judge is validated using human-verified synthetic golden dialogues. Benchmarking 8 LLMs on 1292 conversation turns reveals failure modes hidden by aggregate metrics: models with similar overall scores vary widely in their adherence to individual rules. All models struggle most with ambiguity clarification and Socratic questioning.
